newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: EU-S.AFRICA FREE TRADE PACT MIGHT HIT SWAZI SUGAR.
newsitem.headline: EU-S.AFRICA FREE TRADE PACT MIGHT HIT SWAZI SUGAR.

text.p: Swaziland's sugar industry said on Monday a possible Free Trade Agreement between South Africa and Europe could hold negative implications for the already embattled Swazi industry.
The European Research Office said in a recent report that a Free Trade Agreement could have a "profound effect" on the Swazi industry.

Swaziland Sugar Association general manager Andy Colhoun told Reuters that although sugar would be excluded from a future trade agreement, products containing sugar like confectionary and chocolate could be exempted from import tariffs.
He said this could impact on the Swazi industry -- already battling against South Africa sanctions over alleged dumping of Swazi sugar on the South African domestic market.
"It is my understanding that any Free Trade Agreement between South Africa and the European Union will exclude sugar.
"Sugar containing products particularly confectionary and chocolate might still come in.

"If cheap imports of chocolates and confectionary came into South Africa, it could definitely reduce the volume of sales of those products produced by people like Cadburys and Beacon and therefore could reduce the amount of sugar used by Cadburys in Swaziland," Colhoun said by telephone from Swaziland.
The European Research Office report said about half of Swazi sugar production is used by the local confectionary and soft drinks industry or exported to the regional market -- mainly South Africa.

"Were the EU to secure the elimination of South African duties and non-tariff barriers on sugar and chocolate confectionary, without the issue of EU export and producer subsidies being properly addressed, then:
"This would seriously affect the price of sugar and confectionary products on the South African market and hence the price and market share of Swazi sugar and confectionary prices," the report said.
The South African sugar industry said earlier this year it stood to lose around 275 million through cheap Swazi sugar imports.

In August, the South African Sugar Association pulled the plug on Swaziland, saying the Swazi imports had forced them to cancel Swazi access to training facilities and use of export facilities in the port of Durban.
Sugar contributes some 57 percent of Swazi foreign exchange earnings and accounts for 67 percent of the tiny mountain kingdom's agricultural production.
